# Team strategy

ICPC performance depends on shared state: who owns which problem, when to
switch, how to preserve debugging context, and how to maintain a notebook. The
algorithmic drills here are small but represent team operations: ranking,
balancing, and choosing known templates quickly.

## Shared contest state

The team needs a visible board:

```text
Problem | owner | idea | status | blocker | next action
```

Without this, two people duplicate work or a promising partial idea gets lost
during a switch.

## Ownership rules

Each active problem should have one owner. Other teammates can review, test, or
derive math, but the owner decides when to code and submit. This prevents
half-merged ideas.

Switch ownership when:

- the owner is stuck after a fixed time box;
- a teammate sees a complete solution;
- the problem needs a template another teammate knows better.

## Keyboard management

For one-machine ICPC, the keyboard is a scarce resource. Good teams separate:

- thinking on paper;
- writing tests;
- coding final solutions;
- debugging.

Do not let one long debugging session block all implementation unless the
problem is clearly near accepted.

## Notebook strategy

A good notebook is short and trusted. Include:

- DSU, Fenwick, segment tree;
- Dijkstra, Dinic, SCC/2-SAT;
- geometry primitives;
- KMP/Z/hash;
- CRT, modular inverse, matrix or Fibonacci doubling.

Every template should have a tiny usage note and known indexing convention.

## Communication protocol

When handing off a problem, say:

```text
I think the model is ...
The invariant is ...
The failing case is ...
The next thing to try is ...
```

This is faster than retelling the whole statement.

## Example team board

```text
Problem  Owner  Status        Next action
A        Ana    AC            none
B        Ben    coding        test overflow
C        Chen   idea found    wait for keyboard
D        Ana    reading       decide model
E        none   untouched     scan later
```

This board prevents silent duplication. It also makes it easier to interrupt
work: if Ben leaves the keyboard, the next person knows the current risk.

## Notebook discipline

Do not include a template you do not trust. A shorter notebook with tested code
beats a long notebook full of half-remembered snippets. Every notebook template
should have:

```text
input convention
indexing convention
complexity
one tiny sample use
```

## Handoff example

Bad handoff:

```text
"I tried C, it is weird."
```

Good handoff:

```text
"C looks like bipartite matching. Left side is tasks, right side is people.
The bug is that person capacity is 2, so we either duplicate person nodes or use
flow. I tested the sample graph by hand; max answer should be 4."
```

The second handoff preserves the model, the blocker, and the next action.

## Team debugging roles

When one person codes, the reviewer should not just watch syntax. The reviewer
tracks:

```text
indexing convention
overflow risk
sample walkthrough
unhandled edge cases
whether the code still matches the proof
```

This makes debugging parallel even with one keyboard.

## Contest communication anti-patterns

Avoid:

```text
"It should work."
"The bug is somewhere in the code."
"This is probably DP."
```

Prefer:

```text
"The invariant is prefix parity."
"The failing case is n=1."
"The DP state lacks the previous color."
```

Concrete statements let teammates act.

# Exercises

- A. Team Assignment: Split implementation workload between two people minimizing max time.
- B. Team Scoreboard: Rank teams by contest rules.
- C. Template Fibonacci: Fast recurrence query drill for the team notebook.
# Contest checklist

State the invariant, choose the model, prove the operation, then code the smallest reliable version.
